quests.correctSentence: I like tea and coffee; both wake me up.
quests.contrastSentence: I like tea but coffee; both wake me up.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'And' simply adds one idea to another with no contrast: tea and coffee. 'But' would be needed if the sentence suddenly disliked one of them.
quests.nativeTip: Both drinks are being liked equally here — nothing contrasts.

quests.correctSentence: I like tea, but I don't like coffee at all.
quests.contrastSentence: I like tea, or I don't like coffee at all.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'But' introduces a contrast between two ideas: I like tea, but I don't like coffee. 'And' would only work if both halves agreed with each other.
quests.nativeTip: The second half of the sentence goes against the first half.

quests.correctSentence: — Did you enjoy the trip? — Yes, but it was very tiring by the end.
quests.contrastSentence: — Did you enjoy the trip? — Yes, or it was very tiring by the end.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'But' connects the positive 'enjoyed it' with the less positive 'tiring', showing a contrast within the same experience.
quests.nativeTip: Enjoying something and being tired by it are two slightly opposing ideas.

quests.correctSentence: Would you like tea or coffee?
quests.contrastSentence: Would you like tea and coffee?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Or' presents a choice between alternatives: tea or coffee. 'And' would instead suggest offering both together.
quests.nativeTip: This question offers a choice between two options.

quests.correctSentence: It was raining heavily, so we stayed inside all afternoon.
quests.contrastSentence: It was raining heavily, and we stayed inside all afternoon.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'So' introduces a result or consequence: it rained, so we stayed inside. The staying inside directly happened because of the rain.
quests.nativeTip: The second half is the direct result of the first half.

quests.correctSentence: — Should I call you or text you? — Call me, or text me, either is fine.
quests.contrastSentence: — Should I call you or text you? — Call me, and text me, either is fine.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Or' shows that both options are acceptable alternatives, matching the choice already offered in the question.
quests.nativeTip: The reply offers two equally acceptable options, just like the question did.

quests.correctSentence: I stayed home because I was feeling sick.
quests.contrastSentence: I stayed home so I was feeling sick.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Because' introduces the reason behind an action: stayed home because I was sick. The sickness is the cause, and staying home is the effect.
quests.nativeTip: The second half explains the reason for the first half.

quests.correctSentence: I was feeling sick, so I stayed home.
quests.contrastSentence: I was feeling sick, because I stayed home.
quests.ruleExplanation: When the cause comes first, 'so' introduces the result: was sick, so stayed home. This expresses the same relationship as Question 1, just in reverse order.
quests.nativeTip: Notice the order has flipped from the last question — the cause now comes first.

quests.correctSentence: — Why didn't you come to the meeting? — Because I had a family emergency.
quests.contrastSentence: — Why didn't you come to the meeting? — So I had a family emergency.
quests.ruleExplanation: A question starting with 'why' expects a reason in return, which 'because' introduces directly: Because I had an emergency.
quests.nativeTip: The question asked 'why', which calls for a reason.

quests.correctSentence: Although it was raining, we went for a walk anyway.
quests.contrastSentence: But it was raining, we went for a walk anyway.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Although' introduces an unexpected contrast: although it rained, we still walked. 'But' could express a similar idea, but not at the very start of a sentence like this.
quests.nativeTip: The second half happens despite the first half, not because of it.

quests.equation: Key Form: Although it was raining, we went for a walk.
quests.correctSentence: Which sentence is correct?
quests.contrastSentence: Which sentence is correct?
quests.targetWord: Although it was raining, we went for a walk.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Although' and 'but' both express contrast, so using them together in one sentence is redundant and incorrect. Only one is needed: Although it was raining, we went for a walk.
quests.nativeTip: A sentence usually needs only one connecting word for a single contrast, not two together.

quests.correctSentence: — The movie was long. — Yeah, although it was really long, I enjoyed every minute.
quests.contrastSentence: — The movie was long. — Yeah, so it was really long, I enjoyed every minute.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Although' fits here because it can begin the clause and express the same kind of contrast 'but' would in the middle of a sentence.
quests.nativeTip: Enjoying it despite the length is a contrast, and this word can start the sentence.

quests.correctSentence: When I get home, I'll call you right away.
quests.contrastSentence: If I get home, I'll call you right away.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'When' is used for events that are certain to happen, focusing on timing: when I get home. 'If' would suggest doubt about whether it will happen at all.
quests.nativeTip: Getting home is certain here — it's just a matter of time.

quests.correctSentence: If it rains tomorrow, we'll cancel the picnic.
quests.contrastSentence: Although it rains tomorrow, we'll cancel the picnic.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'If' introduces an uncertain condition: if it rains. This contrasts with 'when', which the last question used for something already expected to happen.
quests.nativeTip: Tomorrow's weather isn't certain — this is a real possibility, not a sure thing.

quests.correctSentence: — Are you sure you'll pass the exam? — I'm not sure, but if I do, I'll celebrate!
quests.contrastSentence: — Are you sure you'll pass the exam? — I'm not sure, but when I do, I'll celebrate!
quests.ruleExplanation: Since the speaker admits uncertainty ('not sure'), the condition needs 'if': if I do, I'll celebrate. 'When' would wrongly suggest passing is already certain.
quests.nativeTip: The words 'not sure' show this outcome isn't guaranteed.

quests.correctSentence: While she was cooking, he set the table.
quests.contrastSentence: When she was cooking, he set the table.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'While' connects two actions happening simultaneously: while she cooked, he set the table. 'Because' would wrongly suggest one action caused the other.
quests.nativeTip: Both actions were happening at the same time.

quests.correctSentence: While my brother loves sports, I prefer reading.
quests.contrastSentence: When my brother loves sports, I prefer reading.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'While' can also mean 'whereas', highlighting a contrast between two people or ideas: while he loves sports, I prefer reading. This is a different use from the simultaneous-action meaning in Question 1.
quests.nativeTip: This isn't about timing here — it's comparing two different preferences.

quests.correctSentence: — What were you doing when I called? — I was studying while my roommate was watching TV.
quests.contrastSentence: — What were you doing when I called? — I was studying when my roommate was watching TV.
quests.ruleExplanation: This describes two simultaneous actions, so 'while' fits: studying while someone else watched TV, echoing the pattern from Question 1.
quests.nativeTip: Two actions were happening at the exact same time, like Question 1.

quests.correctSentence: I won't go to the party unless you come with me.
quests.contrastSentence: I won't go to the party if you come with me.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Unless' means 'except if' or 'only if not': won't go unless you come, meaning I'll go only on the condition that you come too.
quests.nativeTip: This means 'only if you don't come' — a negative condition.

quests.correctSentence: 'Unless you hurry, you'll miss the bus' means the same as: 'If you don't hurry, you'll miss the bus.'
quests.contrastSentence: 'Unless you hurry, you'll miss the bus' means the same as: 'If you do hurry, you'll miss the bus.'
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Unless' is equivalent to 'if...not': unless you hurry means if you don't hurry. This is a useful way to check your understanding of 'unless' by rewriting it with 'if'.
quests.nativeTip: 'Unless' already carries a hidden negative meaning inside it.

quests.correctSentence: — Will you help me move this weekend? — Sure, unless something urgent comes up.
quests.contrastSentence: — Will you help me move this weekend? — Sure, if something urgent comes up.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Unless' sets up the one exception that could cancel the plan: I'll help unless something urgent comes up, meaning the plan stands except in that one case.
quests.nativeTip: The plan is a 'yes', but with one possible exception.

quests.conceptTitle: Sentence Connection: Comma with Subordinate Clauses
quests.grammarRule: Sentence Connection: Comma with Subordinate Clauses
quests.equation: Key Form: Because it was late, we went home.
quests.correctSentence: Which sentence uses punctuation correctly?
quests.contrastSentence: Which sentence uses punctuation correctly?
quests.targetWord: Because it was late, we went home.
quests.ruleExplanation: When a subordinate clause like 'because it was late' starts the sentence, a comma separates it from the main clause: Because it was late, we went home.
quests.nativeTip: When the reason comes first, it usually needs a comma right before the main statement.

quests.conceptTitle: Sentence Connection: Comma with Subordinate Clauses
quests.grammarRule: Sentence Connection: Comma with Subordinate Clauses
quests.equation: Key Form: We went home because it was late.
quests.correctSentence: Which sentence uses punctuation correctly?
quests.contrastSentence: Which sentence uses punctuation correctly?
quests.targetWord: We went home because it was late.
quests.ruleExplanation: When the main clause comes first, no comma is needed before 'because': We went home because it was late. The comma rule from Question 1 only applies when the subordinate clause starts the sentence.
quests.nativeTip: This time the main statement comes first — does the rule from the last question still apply the same way?

quests.conceptTitle: Sentence Connection: Comma with Subordinate Clauses
quests.grammarRule: Sentence Connection: Comma with Subordinate Clauses
quests.equation: Key Form: Although he was tired, he kept working.
quests.correctSentence: Which version is correctly punctuated?
quests.contrastSentence: Which version is correctly punctuated?
quests.targetWord: Although he was tired, he kept working.
quests.ruleExplanation: Since the sentence begins with the subordinate clause 'although he was tired', a comma is needed before the main clause: Although he was tired, he kept working.
quests.nativeTip: 'Although' starts this sentence, so the same comma rule from Question 1 applies here too.

quests.correctSentence: I wanted to go out, but it was raining, so I stayed in.
quests.contrastSentence: I wanted to go out, and it was raining, so I stayed in.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'But' shows the contrast between wanting to go out and the rain stopping that plan, right before 'so' introduces the final result.
quests.nativeTip: This connects a wish with something that got in its way.

quests.correctSentence: She studied hard because she wanted to pass the exam.
quests.contrastSentence: She studied hard although she wanted to pass the exam.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Because' introduces the reason for studying hard: studied because she wanted to pass, matching the reason-and-result pattern from Level 73.
quests.nativeTip: Wanting to pass is the motivation behind the studying.

quests.correctSentence: — Are you coming to the party? — I'd love to, but I have to work that night.
quests.contrastSentence: — Are you coming to the party? — I'd love to, and I have to work that night.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'But' contrasts the wish to attend with the obstacle preventing it: I'd love to, but I have to work. This is a very common everyday pattern for declining politely.
quests.nativeTip: Wanting to come and being unable to are two opposing ideas.

quests.correctSentence: Thank you for your message. Although I understand your concerns, I believe we can resolve this quickly.
quests.contrastSentence: Thank you for your message. Because I understand your concerns, I believe we can resolve this quickly.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Although' softens the message by acknowledging the concern before turning to a positive outcome: although I understand your concerns, we can resolve this. This kind of polite contrast is common in professional writing.
quests.nativeTip: This professional message acknowledges a concern before offering reassurance despite it.

quests.correctSentence: I'll send the invoice today so you can process payment by Friday.
quests.contrastSentence: I'll send the invoice today although you can process payment by Friday.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'So' connects the action (sending the invoice) with its intended result (payment by Friday), a common structure in workplace messages.
quests.nativeTip: Sending the invoice is meant to lead directly to being able to pay by Friday.

quests.correctSentence: — Can we reschedule the call? — Of course! I'm flexible unless something urgent comes up.
quests.contrastSentence: — Can we reschedule the call? — Of course! I'm flexible if something urgent comes up.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Unless' sets the one possible exception to being flexible, exactly as practiced in Level 77: flexible unless something urgent comes up. This wraps up the full run of conjunctions covered across Levels 71 to 80.
quests.nativeTip: This closes Stage 4 the same way Level 77 practiced this exact exception structure.
